answer: In node2vec (Grover and Leskovec, 2016), the return parameter p and in-out parameter q control a biased second-order random walk that interpolates between breadth-first sampling (BFS) and depth-first sampling (DFS). BFS-like walks (small q, or more generally walks that stay within the immediate neighborhood of the source node) sample only nodes at small distances from the start node, so the embeddings they produce encode the local neighborhood structure and tend to place nodes with similar roles or structural positions (structural equivalence, e.g., hubs, bridges, or nodes with similar local connectivity patterns) close together, even if they are far apart in the network. DFS-like walks (large q... in the paper's convention, low q favors outward exploration) travel further away from the source, sampling nodes at increasing distances, so the embeddings capture broader community or homophily structure: nodes in the same tightly knit community, which are close to one another in the network, get similar representations (homophily). Thus DFS captures homophilous equivalence (communities, close network proximity), while BFS captures structural equivalence (similar roles based on local neighborhood topology). In short, BFS plays the central role in representing structural equivalence because its restricted, local exploration of immediate neighbors reflects the local structural roles of nodes, whereas DFS favors the broader, community-level proximity captured by homophily.
